No slides were found for this lecture. The page is built from the doctor's notes (green), every gift (red) and the Aldughaither summary (grey, at the end). Paediatric hernia questions that were filed here are included at the end.

Risk factors & epidemiology

  • Non-modifiable: age (fascial weakness), sex, genetics (strong in young inguinal hernias).
  • Sex: inguinal hernia is much more common in males (the canal transmits the spermatic cord). Femoral hernia is relatively more common in females — classically older, thin women (the femoral canal's fat is lost).
  • Modifiable: obesity (ventral/incisional), smoking (incisional, poor healing), ↑ intra-abdominal pressure (pregnancy, constipation, chronic cough, heavy lifting), COPD, diabetes, steroids, biologics, collagen disorders, multiple pregnancies.
Inguinal hernia = the most common hernia overall (in both sexes).
GroupKey point (doctor)
Young men (teens/20s)Congenital/genetic — ~50% have a first-degree relative
Men > ~50Acquired weakness
Elderly men 70–80Prevalence ~20%
Lifetime risk~27% men vs ~3% women by 80
FemoralProportionally more common in women
Saudi ArabiaUmbilical/periumbilical more common in females
IncisionalIncreasingly common (multiple operations, obesity, smoking)
  • Pitfall: CT shows an abdominal-wall defect in ~1 in 5 people — a defect ≠ a clinical hernia (needs protrusion). Don't repair incidental CT defects.
  • Most common hernia in a 55-year-old woman → inguinal 438; in a 60-year-old Saudi man → keyed indirect inguinal. 438 ×2
  • Femoral hernia — true → keyed "it has the highest complication rate" (narrow rigid neck → strangulation); it isn't the commonest hernia in females and lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. 427 ×2

Anatomy

  • Rectus abdominis inside the anterior and posterior sheath; the posterior sheath ends at the arcuate line; lateral muscles (external oblique, internal oblique, transversus) meet at the linea semilunaris. The umbilicus is a natural weak point (old cord opening).
  • Abdominal wall layers, superficial → deep → skin, superficial fascia, external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis, transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal fat, peritoneum. 438

Direct vs indirect inguinal hernia

The inferior epigastric vessels separate them: lateral = indirect, medial = direct.
IndirectDirect
EntryDeep inguinal ringPosterior wall — Hesselbach's triangle
Relation to inferior epigastric vesselsLateralMedial
Reaches scrotum?YesLess typically
AssociationCongenital (patent processus vaginalis), youngerAcquired weakness, older
  • Hesselbach's triangle: lateral border of rectus (medial), inferior epigastric vessels (lateral), inguinal ligament (inferior).
  • Structure that differentiates direct from indirect → inferior epigastric vessels 439; direct hernia → medial to the inferior epigastric artery. 427 ×3
  • Direct hernia — the false statement → "penetrates the fascia iliacus" (a direct hernia pushes through the transversalis fascia of the posterior wall). 426
  • Groin swelling in a 32-year-old not descending to the scrotum → keyed indirect hernia (commonest at every age). 439
  • Hernia that protrudes through the superficial ring with a cough impulse → direct or indirect (both can). 438
  • Defect causing indirect inguinal hernia in children → patent processus vaginalis. 439

Types of abdominal wall hernia

  • Groin: inguinal (direct/indirect), femoral · umbilical/ventral · epigastric (decussation of linea alba fibres; pregnancy, obesity) · incisional · parastomal · Spigelian (between lateral muscle layers — often non-palpable, needs CT/MRI) · obturator (rare).
  • Port-site hernias: 5 mm very unlikely; 10–15 mm → close the fascia (ports ≥ 10 mm).
  • Epigastric hernia → usually small in size (often contains only fat). 438
  • All pass through an aponeurosis except → keyed umbilical hernia (passes through the umbilical scar/ring itself). 427 ×2
  • Richter's hernia → only part of the circumference of the bowel wall is trapped (can strangulate without obstruction). 426

Clinical presentation & examination

  • Bulge and pain/discomfort (pulling, heaviness — typically after walking ~10–15 min), worse with cough, straining, lifting, standing. Diffuse or severe pain → think of a complication.
A bulge that comes and goes (reducible) and enlarges with cough/strain strongly suggests a hernia. Hernia is a clinical diagnosis.
  • History: location, duration/progression, pain, reducibility, relation to cough/activity, previous operation (incisional), previous repair (recurrence), quality of life.
  • Examine standing first (it may disappear supine). Most important question: reducible or not? Then consistency, tenderness, defect, cough impulse. A firm, fixed, unusual, non-reducible mass → doubt the diagnosis.
  • Sign most important to confirm an inguinal hernia → positive cough impulse. 436
  • 50-year-old man, groin bulge enlarging on standing and coughing → inguinal hernia. 441

Imaging

  • Most hernias are diagnosed clinically — "Will this investigation change my management?"
Imaging helps when…Why
Diagnostic uncertaintyAtypical, firm, irreducible, immobile lesion
Incisional herniaCT — defects, contents, approach
Recurrent herniaDistorted planes, mesh location
Large/complex herniaApproach, mesh, component separation, Botox
  • 4-year-old with a thickened right cord and positive cough impulse (both testes down) → no imaging required (clinical diagnosis). 436

Management

  • Why repair: symptoms/quality of life · prevent progression (a 1-hour laparoscopic repair can become a major reconstruction) · prevent complications (incarceration → obstruction → strangulation).
  • Watchful waiting: small/minimally symptomatic hernia or poor surgical candidate (severe IHD, home-oxygen COPD, anticoagulation, frail). Major complication risk ≈ 1–2%/year. Patients must know the red flags.
  • Optimize before elective repair: smoking, obesity (e.g. BMI 45 with failed repairs → lose weight first), diabetes, cough.
  • Hernia belt/truss = symptom relief only — doesn't cure or stop progression (reduce first, then apply).
LaparoscopicOpen
AdvantagesLess wound infection, less painSuits many straightforward hernias
FavouredObesity, smoking, bilateral, femoral, recurrence after open/anterior meshRecurrence after laparoscopic repair, high anaesthetic risk
AnaesthesiaGeneralCan be local, regional, spinal
Recurrence → use the other approach: previous open repair → laparoscopic; previous laparoscopic → open.
  • Recurrent right inguinal hernia 3 years after open repair → laparoscopic mesh repair. 439 ×4
  • Nerves at risk in inguinal hernia repair → ilioinguinal, iliohypogastric, genitofemoral. 438 ×4
  • Local-anaesthetic repair — nerve usually blocked → iliohypogastric (with ilioinguinal). 429
  • Cirrhosis with ascites and a fat-containing hernia → control the ascites, then repair (ascites drives recurrence and leaks). 441

Mesh

Elective clean repair → mesh (lower recurrence). Emergency with bowel resection/contamination → tissue repair (avoid infected mesh), accepting more recurrence.
  • Strangulated hernia with bowel resection and primary anastomosis → herniorrhaphy (tissue repair, no mesh). 426
  • Hernia contents: omentum (ischaemia → pain/inflammation, less dangerous) or bowel (incarceration → obstruction → strangulation); rarely bladder, ovary, kidney.

Complications

StageDefinitionFeatures
1. IncarcerationNon-reducible; blood supply initially intactPain, but the patient may walk and eat normally
2. ObstructionTrapped bowel lumen blockedPain, vomiting, distension, obstipation
3. StrangulationBlood supply compromised → ischaemia → necrosisSevere pain, marked tenderness, red/warm skin, fever, leukocytosis, sepsis
An acute painful irreducible hernia is treated urgently — incarceration and early strangulation are hard to tell apart. Obvious strangulation → OR; don't delay for imaging ("time is tissue").
  • At surgery: release the constriction → warm the bowel → allow reperfusion → reassess → resect non-viable bowel.
  • Woman, bulge below the inguinal ligament, now irreducible with no flatus for a day, no skin change → incarcerated femoral hernia 441 ×9; known reducible inguinal hernia, painful 16 h with distension and vomiting → strangulated. 435 ×8
  • Strangulation = ischaemia of the protruded organs 426; a strangulated hernia is an extramural cause of obstruction. 439
  • Young man with no previous surgery, SBO → first examine the groins. 438 ×10

Paediatric hernias (from past exams)

Infant inguinal hernia → herniotomy as early as possible (high incarceration risk) — no mesh (only the patent sac is ligated). Umbilical hernia in children → most close spontaneously; repair at ~4–5 years if persisting (or earlier if large).
  • 2-month-old girl, reducible left groin swelling → herniotomy as early as possible 439 ×7; child with an inguinal hernia seen by a GP → refer to a paediatric surgeon. 435
  • Father wants mesh for his 3-month-old → mesh isn't required — herniotomy only. 438
  • 2-month-old with bilateral hernia and hydrocele → bilateral hernia repair and evacuation of the hydrocele. 434
  • 2-year-old: hernia irreducible 6 h, no skin change → incarcerated inguinal hernia 439 ×3; incarcerated hernia in a 3-month-old → trial of reduction under sedation/analgesia (then herniotomy after 24–48 h) 435 ×8; what separates elective from emergency → reducibility. 435
  • Boy, reducible lump into the scrotum, positive internal-ring occlusion test → indirect inguinal hernia. 436
  • 5-month-old reducible umbilical hernia → repair at 4–5 years if not resolved 438 ×4; 5-year-old with a 1-cm umbilical defect since birth → surgical repair (unlikely to close now). 439 ×3

Abdominal Wall Hernias

Hernias

A hernia is the abnormal protrusion of intra-abdominal contents through a weakened area or defect in the muscle or fascia of the abdominal wall.

Key Components of a Hernia:

1. Hernia sac – Peritoneal lining containing the herniated contents.

2. Hernia contents – May include preperitoneal fat, omentum, bowel, or

  • other organs.

3. Hernia covering – Layers of skin, subcutaneous tissue, and muscle over the

  • defect.

Hernias may be congenital (present at birth) or acquired (develop later in life).

Classification of Hernias
1. Based on Location
  • Groin Hernias (~75%)
  • Inguinal Hernia (most common type).
  • Femoral Hernia (higher risk of strangulation).
  • Ventral Hernias (~25%)
  • Umbilical Hernia (around the navel).
  • Epigastric Hernia (between the umbilicus and xiphoid process).
  • Incisional Hernia (occurs at a previous surgical incision).
  • Spigelian Hernia (at the semilunar line).
  • Rare Hernias
  • Obturator Hernia (through the obturator foramen).
  • Lumbar Hernia (at the lumbar triangle).
  • Richter’s Hernia (only part of the bowel circumference is trapped).
2. Based on Reducibility
  • Reducible Hernia – Hernia contents return to the abdomen spontaneously or with gentle pressure.
  • Incarcerated Hernia – Hernia contents cannot be reduced due to being trapped.
  • Obstructed Hernia – Hernia causes bowel obstruction but no blood supply compromise.
  • Strangulated Hernia – Hernia compromises blood supply, leading to ischemia and necrosis.
Clinical Presentation
Symptoms
  • Groin or abdominal mass/bulge, which may:
  • Increase in size with straining, coughing, or standing.
  • Disappear when lying down (if reducible).
  • Pain or discomfort (especially with activity or heavy lifting).
  • Nausea, vomiting, and abdominal distension (if obstruction or strangulation occurs).
Physical Examination
  • Palpable mass at the site of the hernia.
  • Assess reducibility:
  • If reducible → Returns to the abdomen with pressure.
  • If incarcerated → Does not return with pressure.
  • Bowel sounds:
  • Hyperactive in obstruction.
  • Absent in strangulation.
  • Skin changes (erythema, tenderness, warmth) → Suggests strangulation or infection.
Diagnostic Workup
1. Clinical Examination
  • Most hernias are diagnosed based on history and physical examination.
2. Imaging
  • Ultrasound → Best for detecting inguinal and femoral hernias.
  • CT scan → Best for complex, incisional, or strangulated hernias.
  • MRI → Used for occult (hidden) hernias.
Management of Hernias
1. Conservative Management
  • Observation → In small, asymptomatic hernias.
  • Supportive measures:
  • Avoid heavy lifting and straining.
  • Use of abdominal binders in poor surgical candidates.
2. Surgical Treatment (Definitive)
Indications for Surgery:
  • Symptomatic hernias (pain, discomfort, increasing size).
  • Incarcerated hernias (to prevent strangulation).
  • Strangulated hernias (emergency surgery to prevent necrosis).
Types of Surgical Repair
1. Open Hernia Repair (e.g., Lichtenstein technique)
  • Hernia is reduced, and a synthetic mesh is placed to reinforce the defect.
  • Best for large or recurrent hernias.

2. Laparoscopic Hernia Repair

  • Less pain, faster recovery, fewer complications.
  • Preferred for bilateral or recurrent inguinal hernias.
  • Techniques include TAPP (transabdominal preperitoneal) and TEP (totally extraperitoneal) approaches.
Complications of Untreated Hernias
  • Bowel Obstruction → Intestinal blockage due to incarceration.
  • Strangulation → Compromised blood supply leading to necrosis.
  • Peritonitis → Infection spreading into the peritoneal cavity.
  • Chronic Pain → Due to nerve compression.
Groin Hernias
Overview

Groin hernias occur when intra-abdominal contents protrude through a defect in the myopectineal orifice of Fruchaud, a weak area in the transversalis fascia of the groin. They account for ~75% of all abdominal wall hernias and include:

  • Inguinal hernias (Indirect & Direct).
  • Femoral hernias (higher risk of strangulation).
Anatomy of the Groin and Hernia Sites

The inguinal region consists of multiple muscular and fascial layers that contribute to hernia formation and repair.

Key Structures in the Groin:
  • Transversalis fascia – The primary site of weakness in direct inguinal hernias.
  • Hesselbach’s Triangle – Bordered by the inguinal ligament, inferior epigastric vessels, and rectus abdominis. This is the site of direct inguinal hernias.
  • Inguinal Canal – Contains the spermatic cord (males) or round ligament (females). Indirect hernias pass through this canal.
  • Femoral Canal – Space beneath the inguinal ligament medial to the femoral vein, where femoral hernias occur.
Types of Groin Hernias
1. Inguinal Hernias (~96% of Groin Hernias)

These occur above the inguinal ligament and can be direct or indirect.

Pantaloon Hernia: A combined direct + indirect inguinal hernia, with peritoneum protruding on both sides of the inferior epigastric vessels.

2. Femoral Hernias (~4% of Groin Hernias)

Occurs below the inguinal ligament, passing through the femoral ring (bounded by lacunar ligament medially and femoral vein laterally).

  • More common in women.
  • Highest risk of strangulation (due to narrow canal).
  • Presents as a painful groin mass below the inguinal ligament.
Clinical Presentation
Symptoms
  • Groin bulge/mass, which:
  • Increases with standing, straining, coughing.
  • May be reducible or incarcerated.
  • Pain or discomfort (especially with prolonged activity).
  • Nausea, vomiting, distension (suggests obstruction or strangulation).
Physical Examination
  • Palpate for a bulge in the groin while the patient stands and coughs.
  • Indirect hernia: Bulge felt at deep inguinal ring (lateral to inferior epigastric vessels).
  • Direct hernia: Bulge felt at Hesselbach’s Triangle (medial to inferior epigastric vessels).
  • Femoral hernia: Bulge below the inguinal ligament.
Diagnosis

1. Clinical Examination (Most cases diagnosed this way).

  • Valsalva maneuver – Increases intra-abdominal pressure to detect hernias.
  • Examine in standing and supine positions.
2. Imaging (if unclear diagnosis)
  • Ultrasound → Best for detecting inguinal and femoral hernias.
  • CT Scan → Best for complex or strangulated hernias.
  • MRI → Used for occult (hidden) hernias.
Management
  • As mentioned above including the conservative and surgical approaches.
Indirect & Direct Inguinal Hernias
Clinical Findings
A. Symptoms
  • Most hernias are initially asymptomatic – Patients may first notice a lump or swelling in the groin.
  • Sudden pain and bulge during lifting or straining (common presentation).
  • Dragging sensation or aching pain (especially with indirect hernias, pain may radiate to the scrotum).
  • Discomfort relieved by manual reduction of the hernia.
B. Physical Examination
  • Inspect the patient both supine & standing.
  • Ask the patient to perform a Valsalva maneuver (coughing or straining can make small hernias more apparent).
  • Differentiate between hernia types:
  • Indirect Hernia → Felt at the tip of the examining finger upon invaginating the scrotum.
  • Direct Hernia → Impulse felt on the side of the finger when pushing into the inguinal canal.
  • Femoral Hernia → Lies below the inguinal ligament, lateral to the pubic tubercle.
  • Direct hernias produce a symmetric, circular bulge.
  • Indirect hernias appear as an elongated, elliptical swelling following the inguinal canal.
Note: The posterior wall of the inguinal canal is:
  • Firm & resistant in indirect hernias.
  • Weak or absent in direct hernias.
Differential Diagnosis
Several conditions may mimic an inguinal hernia:

Diagnostic Clues:
  • Irreducible mass + cough impulse → Likely a hernia.
  • Transillumination (fluid-filled mass) → Likely a hydrocele.
  • Bowel sounds in the mass → Suggest a hernia with possible bowel involvement.
Treatment of Inguinal Hernias
1. Observation (Non-Surgical Management)
  • Asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic hernias in elderly, sedentary patients may be observed.
  • Annual risk of incarceration is low (~0.2%), but symptoms often worsen over time.
However, surgery is generally recommended to prevent complications.
2. Surgical Treatment (Definitive Management)
Indications for Surgery
  • All symptomatic inguinal hernias.
  • Incarcerated hernias (urgent surgery if irreducible).
  • Strangulated hernias (emergency surgery required to prevent necrosis).
Surgical Techniques

(Tension-Based)tissue repair
Bassini RepairSuturing of transversalis fasciaRarely used today
  • Mesh repair significantly reduces recurrence rates.
  • Laparoscopic repair results in quicker recovery & less pain but requires expertise.
3. Management of Incarcerated or Strangulated Hernias
Incarcerated Hernia (Urgent Repair)
  • Attempt gentle manual reduction with sedation & Trendelenburg positioning.
  • DO NOT reduce if signs of strangulation (pain, erythema, peritonitis, sepsis).
Strangulated Hernia (Emergency Surgery)
  • Immediate exploration required.
  • Signs of bowel ischemia (dark, bloody fluid in sac) → May require bowel resection.
  • Laparoscopy can help assess bowel viability.

Preoperative Considerations
  • Groin hernia repair is usually an outpatient procedure, but a thorough preoperative evaluation should be performed before surgery.
  • Anesthesia Options:
  • Local anesthesia → Best for most patients; lowers risk of urinary retention & pulmonary complications.
  • Spinal or general anesthesia → Preferred for recurrent hernias (due to scarring). ✔ Activity Post-Surgery:
  • Sedentary workers → Can return to work within a few days.
  • Manual laborers → Traditionally advised to wait 4-6 weeks, but recent studies suggest resuming activity as early as 2 weeks is safe, especially if mesh is used.
Postoperative Prognosis & Recurrence Risk
Factors contributing to hernia recurrence:
  • Chronic cough, prostate enlargement, constipation (increase intra- abdominal pressure).
  • Poor tissue quality (more common in direct hernias).
  • Technical errors in surgery, such as:
  • Failure to fully dissect the hernia sac.
  • Not covering the internal ring adequately.
  • Placing excessive tension on the repair.
  • Postoperative wound infection increases recurrence risk.
Patient factors associated with higher recurrence:
  • Chronic peritoneal dialysis patients.
  • Cirrhotic patients with ascites.
  • Smokers.
  • Patients on steroids or who are malnourished.
Current recurrence rates:
  • Best surgical techniques report a 4% recurrence rate.
  • Failure to recognize a coexisting femoral or indirect hernia increases recurrence risk.
Chronic Groin Pain After Hernia Repair

Chronic groin pain is an underappreciated complication of hernia repair (~5-6% incidence).

  • Causes of Chronic Groin Pain:
  • 1️- Recurrent hernia.
  • 2️- Mesh-related irritation or inflammation.
  • 3️- Nerve entrapment or neuroma (ilioinguinal nerve is most involved).
Strategies to Reduce Postoperative Pain:
  • Laparoscopic repair has a lower risk of chronic pain.
  • Prophylactic division of the ilioinguinal nerve during open repair may help.
  • Discussion of chronic pain risk should be included in informed consent.
Nonsurgical Management: Use of a Truss
When is a Truss Used?
  • For patients who decline surgery.
  • Absolute contraindications to surgery (e.g., severe comorbidities).
Proper Use of a Truss:
  • Should provide firm compression over the hernia defect.
  • Worn during the day, removed at night.
  • Applied before standing in the morning.
Limitations of Truss Use:
  • Does NOT cure a hernia.
  • May cause fibrosis, making future surgical repair more difficult.
Sliding Inguinal Hernia

Sliding inguinal hernia is a type of indirect inguinal hernia in which a portion of a hollow viscus (organ) forms part of the hernia sac wall.

Commonly involved organs:
  • Right side → Cecum (most frequent).
  • Left side → Sigmoid colon (most frequent).
  • Other possible structures → Bladder, ovary, retroperitoneal ileum.

Cause: Related to the degree of posterior fixation of the organ and its proximity to the internal inguinal ring.

Clinical Findings & Diagnosis
  • No unique signs distinguish sliding hernias from regular inguinal hernias.
  • Should be suspected in large hernias that are difficult to fully reduce.
  • Strong diagnostic clue:
  • Radiographic imaging → A contrast study showing a segment of the colon or bladder within the scrotum.
Intraoperative Importance:
  • Failure to recognize a sliding hernia increases the risk of bowel or bladder injury during surgery.
Treatment of Sliding Inguinal Hernia

Surgical repair is similar to standard inguinal hernia repair, with additional precautions.

Key surgical steps:

1️- Careful dissection of the spermatic cord from the hernia sac.

2️- Recognizing that the posterior wall of the sac consists of colon, bladder, or retroperitoneal structures.

3️- Reduction Techniques:

  • Bevan technique → Uses inverting sutures to reduce the sliding organ.
  • La Roque technique (for large hernias) → Requires a separate peritoneal incision, pulling the bowel back into the abdomen, and securing it to the posterior abdominal wall.
  • Laparoscopic Repair (TAPP/TEP) Possible:
  • Requires an experienced surgeon due to the higher risk of visceral injury.
Prognosis & Complications
  • Higher recurrence rate compared to simple indirect hernias.
  • Biggest surgical risk:
  • Accidental entry into the bowel or bladder due to failure to recognize the sliding hernia.
Femoral Hernia

A femoral hernia occurs when intra-abdominal contents protrude through the femoral canal beneath the inguinal ligament.

Key Features:
  • More common in women but still less frequent than inguinal hernias.
  • Comprise ~33% of groin hernias in women and ~2% of groin hernias in men.
  • Prone to incarceration & strangulation due to its narrow neck.
Clinical Presentation
Symptoms:
  • Often asymptomatic until incarceration or strangulation occurs.
  • Patients may experience abdominal pain rather than groin pain.
  • Obstruction symptoms (colicky pain, nausea, vomiting, distension) may be the first sign.
  • High suspicion needed in patients with intestinal obstruction & no prior abdominal surgeries.
Signs:
  • Small, tender mass in the upper medial thigh, just below the inguinal ligament.
  • May be confused with an inguinal hernia if the hernia is deflected anteriorly.
  • Can be difficult to detect until it becomes incarcerated or strangulated.
Differential Diagnosis
Conditions mimicking femoral hernia:
  • Inguinal hernia → Lies above the inguinal ligament, whereas femoral hernia is below.
  • Saphenous varix → Compressible, disappears on lying down, transmits a thrill on coughing.
  • Femoral adenopathy (lymph node swelling) → non-reducible, often tender with infection.
Treatment

Surgical Repair is Required → Femoral hernias do not resolve spontaneously and have a high risk of incarceration & strangulation.

Surgical Approaches:

1️- Open Repair:

  • Traditional McVay (Cooper Ligament) Repair → Uses sutured repair with a relaxing incision in the anterior rectus sheath.
  • Mesh-Based Open Repair (Preferred) → Reduces recurrence risk.
2️- Laparoscopic Repair:
  • Preperitoneal Mesh Repair (TAPP/TEP techniques) → Minimally invasive, effective in bilateral or recurrent cases.
  • Laparoscopic repair allows for intra-abdominal evaluation in cases of suspected bowel strangulation.
Difficult Reduction?
  • May require careful incision of the iliopubic tract, Gimbernat ligament, or inguinal ligament.
  • Rarely, a counter-incision in the thigh is needed.
If Bloody Fluid in Hernia Sac?
  • Strong suspicion of nonviable bowel → Mandatory intra-abdominal exploration.
Prognosis & Recurrence
  • Recurrence rate: Like inguinal hernias (~4-5%).
  • Timely surgical intervention prevents complications like bowel necrosis & peritonitis.
Umbilical Hernia

Umbilical hernia occurs due to failure of the umbilical fascial ring to properly fuse after birth.

In children, the umbilical ring naturally closes by age 4 in most cases.

In adults, risk factors for umbilical hernia development include:

  • Multiple pregnancies with prolonged labor.
  • Obesity (increased intra-abdominal pressure).
  • Ascites (cirrhosis-related or other causes).
  • Large intra-abdominal tumors.
Clinical Presentation
Symptoms:
  • Painless bulge at the umbilicus, usually enlarging over time.
  • Sharp pain on coughing, straining, or lifting (due to tight hernia ring).
  • Dragging or aching sensation, especially in large hernias.
  • Risk of incarceration & strangulation → Narrow defect increases the risk.
Signs:
  • Round, soft, or firm mass at the umbilicus.
  • May be reducible (contents return into the abdomen).
  • Signs of strangulation (emergency):
  • Severe pain, erythema, non-reducibility, obstruction symptoms (nausea, vomiting, distension).
Treatment
Surgical Repair is the Definitive Treatment
  • Elective repair for reducible hernias with fatty tissue contents.
  • Urgent repair if bowel is involved to prevent obstruction & strangulation.
Repair Techniques:

1️- Suture-only repair → Suitable for small hernias (<2 cm) in low-risk patients.

2️- Mesh-based repair (preferred for large defects) → Lower recurrence rate.

  • Recommended for large hernias, obese patients, heavy laborers, steroid users, or bodybuilders.

3- Minimally invasive (laparoscopic) repair → Less postoperative pain, faster recovery.

Special Considerations:
  • Cirrhosis with ascites is NOT an absolute contraindication to surgery.
  • First manage ascites (medical therapy or transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS)).
  • Optimize fluid/electrolytes & nutrition preoperatively to reduce surgical risks.
Prognosis & Recurrence
Risk factors for recurrence & complications:
  • Large hernia size.
  • Elderly, debilitated patients.
  • Obesity, immunosuppression, or intra-abdominal disease.

In healthy individuals, umbilical hernia repair has a high success rate with low recurrence.

Epigastric Hernia

Epigastric hernias protrude through the linea alba above the umbilicus.

They develop through congenital weaknesses in the linea alba or through foramina of small paramidline vessels and nerves.

Incidence:
  • Occurs in 3%-5% of the population.
  • More common in men than women.
  • Most common between ages 20-50.
  • 20% are multiple, and 80% occur just off the midline.
Clinical Presentation
Symptoms:
  • Mostly asymptomatic, often found incidentally on examination.
  • If symptomatic, patients may report:
  • Mild epigastric pain and tenderness.
  • Deep, burning epigastric pain that radiates to the back or lower abdomen.
  • Bloating, nausea, or vomiting, often after a large meal.
  • Pain relief when reclining, as the herniated contents reduce back into the abdomen.
  • Small hernias (often containing only preperitoneal fat):
  • More prone to incarceration & strangulation → often tender.
  • Larger hernias (may contain omentum, rarely bowel):
  • Less likely to strangulate but may cause discomfort.
Signs:
  • Palpable epigastric mass that protrudes with increased intra-abdominal pressure (e.g., Valsalva).
  • Most located just above the umbilicus.
  • Difficult to detect in obese patients → may require ultrasound or CT scan.
Differential Diagnosis
Gastrointestinal Conditions:
  • Peptic ulcer disease
  • Gallbladder disease
  • Hiatal hernia
  • Pancreatitis
  • Upper small bowel obstruction
Soft Tissue Lesions:
  • Subcutaneous lipoma, fibroma, neurofibroma
Diastasis Recti (NOT a hernia)
  • Diffuse widening of the linea alba without a fascial defect.
  • Appears as a linear, fusiform bulge between rectus muscles with Valsalva.
  • NO risk of incarceration → repair is often avoided due to high recurrence rates.
  • Can be repaired with open or laparoscopic plication techniques if highly symptomatic.
Treatment
Surgical Repair is Recommended for Symptomatic Hernias
  • Same approach as umbilical hernia repair.
  • Small defects → Can be closed with sutures alone.
  • Larger defects or high-risk patients → Mesh repair preferred to lower recurrence.
  • Herniated fat is dissected and removed.

Minimally invasive (laparoscopic) approaches are preferred for faster recovery and less postoperative pain.

Prognosis
  • Good outcomes with repair.
  • Risk of recurrence increases with:
  • Large hernias
  • Obesity
  • Smoking, steroid use, or poor tissue quality
  • Surgery is generally successful, with low complication rates.
Ventral & Incisional Hernias

Incisional hernias occur at previous surgical incision sites and are a common complication of abdominal surgery.

Incidence:
  • Occurs in 10%-30% of all abdominal operations.
  • Risk does not appear to be decreasing, especially with rising obesity rates.
  • Large or complex ventral hernias require more advanced repair techniques.
  • Key Risk Factors:
  • Obesity, diabetes, smoking
  • Wound infection or poor surgical technique
  • Increased intra-abdominal pressure (e.g., chronic coughing, ascites, straining)
  • Collagen defects or metabolic disorders affecting wound healing
Etiology & Risk Factors

The likelihood of incisional hernia increases when multiple risk factors coexist.

1️- Surgical Factors:
  • Poor surgical technique (inadequate fascial closure, excessive tension).
  • Wound infection (80% risk of hernia formation).
  • Failure to close laparoscopic trocar sites >10mm.
  • Large intraoperative blood loss (>1000mL).
2️- Patient-Related Factors:
  • Obesity (increased intra-abdominal pressure, delayed healing).
  • Diabetes (poor microvascular circulation, increased infection risk).
  • Smoking (poor wound healing, increased tissue breakdown).
  • Age & frailty (reduced tissue elasticity).
  • Chronic coughing or straining (COPD, constipation, urinary obstruction).
Clinical Presentation
Symptoms:
  • Visible or palpable abdominal bulge at a previous surgical site.
  • Mild discomfort or pain, which increases with activity.
  • Worsening symptoms with straining, lifting, or prolonged standing.
  • If incarcerated or strangulated → severe pain, tenderness, redness, bowel obstruction symptoms (nausea, vomiting, distension).
Signs:
  • Soft, reducible mass at a prior surgical incision site.
  • Non-reducible or painful hernias may indicate incarceration.
  • Overlying skin changes (redness, ulceration) suggest strangulation.
Indications for Surgery
  • All symptomatic hernias should be repaired to prevent complications.
  • Elective repair for reducible, asymptomatic hernias.
  • Emergency surgery is required for:
  • Incarcerated hernia (cannot be reduced).
  • Obstruction (abdominal distension, vomiting).
  • Strangulation (severe pain, skin changes, systemic signs).
Surgical Treatment Options
1- Suture Repair (Primary Closure)
  • Used only for small defects (<2 cm).
  • High recurrence rates (~30%) if used alone without mesh.
2- Mesh Repair (Standard of Care)
  • Reduces recurrence rates significantly.
  • Mesh Types:
  • Permanent synthetic mesh (polypropylene, polyester).
  • Biologic mesh (porcine or human dermis) → preferred in contaminated/infected fields.
3- Component Separation (For Large Defects)
  • Used when fascial closure cannot be achieved without excessive tension.
  • Techniques:
  • External oblique release (most common).
  • Transversus abdominis release (TAR) for very large defects.
4- Minimally Invasive (Laparoscopic & Robotic) Repair
  • Advantages:
  • Less postoperative pain, faster recovery.
  • Lower risk of wound infections.
  • Limitations:
  • Not ideal for very large hernias or loss of domain cases.
  • Risk of bowel adhesions/fistula formation if uncoated mesh is used.
Prognosis & Recurrence
  • Mesh repair has a lower recurrence rate than suture-only repair.
  • Despite improvements, recurrence remains a significant issue (~4%-30%).
  • Recurrence Risk Factors:
  • Obesity
  • Smoking
  • Diabetes
  • Prior hernia repairs (each reoperation increases recurrence risk).
Preoperative Optimization to Reduce Recurrence:
  • Weight loss before surgery.
  • Diabetes control.
  • Smoking cessation (≥1 month before surgery).
  • Nutritional optimization (especially in malnourished patients).
Parastomal Hernias

Definition: A parastomal hernia is a type of incisional hernia that occurs adjacent to a stoma, where intra-abdominal contents protrude through the fascial opening created for the stoma.

Incidence:
  • Reported in up to 50% of stoma patients.
  • Risk increases over time due to progressive stretching of the fascial defect. ✔ Pathophysiology:
  • A stoma itself is a controlled hernia, and parastomal hernias occur when the fascial defect enlarges, allowing additional bowel or omentum to herniate alongside the stoma.
  • Risk factors mirror those of ventral hernias, including obesity, increased intra-abdominal pressure, collagen defects, and immunosuppression.
Risk Factors
Surgical Factors
  • Improper stoma placement: Stomas should be placed through the rectus muscle (rather than laterally) to reduce hernia risk.
  • Excessive fascial defect size: A too-large opening increases hernia formation.
  • Poor wound healing: Prior infection or ischemia at the stoma site increases risk.
Patient Factors
  • Obesity: Increases intra-abdominal pressure and weakens fascial closure.
  • Chronic straining: Coughing, constipation, or heavy lifting stretches the stoma opening.
  • Malnutrition or steroid use: Collagen synthesis defects impair wound healing.
  • Immunosuppression: Common in transplant and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients.
Clinical Presentation
Symptoms
  • Bulging or lump at the stoma site.
  • Pain or discomfort, worsened by activity.
  • Intermittent obstruction symptoms (bloating, nausea, difficulty passing stool/gas).
  • Difficulty applying the ostomy appliance due to distortion of the stoma.
Signs of Complications
  • Bowel obstruction → Requires urgent evaluation!
  • Strangulation → Surgical emergency!
  • Severe pain, tenderness, or skin discoloration over the hernia.
  • Firm, non-reducible mass.
  • Nausea, vomiting, and bloating (bowel obstruction).
Indications for Surgical Repair
When to Consider Surgery:
  • Symptomatic hernias that cause pain, obstruction, or difficulty with stoma function.
  • Hernias that continue to enlarge, impacting quality of life.
  • Obstructed or strangulated hernias → Emergency surgery required!
When to Observe:
  • Asymptomatic, small parastomal hernias can be monitored.
  • Patients with significant comorbidities who are at high risk for surgery.
Surgical Treatment Options
1- Stoma Reversal (Best Option if Feasible)
  • Closing the stoma and restoring bowel continuity eliminates the need for a fascial defect.
  • Preferred when feasible, but not an option for permanent stomas.
2- Open or Minimally Invasive (MIS) Hernia Repair
  • Mesh-based techniques reduce recurrence.
  • Various approaches exist depending on defect size, prior repairs, and surgeon expertise.
Surgical Techniques:
  • Keyhole Repair
  • Mesh is cut around the stoma, allowing bowel passage while reinforcing the defect.
  • High recurrence rates (~30%) due to mesh tension around the stoma.
  • Sugarbaker Repair (Preferred for Laparoscopic Repair)
  • The stoma is laterally positioned with a large mesh overlay covering the defect.
  • Lower recurrence rates (~10%) compared to Keyhole repair.
  • Cruciate Repair
  • A slit is made in the mesh, with bowel passed through a cross- shaped opening.
  • Alternative to Keyhole repair with similar recurrence rates (~25%- 30%).
  • Retromuscular Repair (Best for Open Surgery)
  • Hernia is repaired in the Retromuscular (Rives-Stoppa) plane with mesh.
  • Low recurrence (~10%) but requires major dissection.
3- Prophylactic Mesh at Initial Stoma Creation (Emerging Best Practice)
  • Prevents hernia formation rather than repairing it later.
  • Studies show a significant reduction in hernia risk (~50% reduction).
  • Not widely adopted in North America but is common in Europe.
Prognosis & Recurrence
Key Factors Affecting Recurrence:
  • Technique used: Mesh-based repairs have a lower recurrence than suture- only repairs.
  • Obesity & straining: Increase hernia recurrence risk.
  • Prior failed hernia repairs: Each reoperation increases recurrence risk.
  • Stoma type: Colostomy has a higher recurrence risk than ileostomy.
Recurrence Rates by Repair Type
  • Primary suture repair: ~100% recurrence (not recommended).
  • Keyhole repair: ~30% recurrence.
  • Sugarbaker repair: ~10% recurrence (preferred laparoscopic approach).
  • Retromuscular mesh repair: ~10% recurrence (best open technique).
  • Prophylactic mesh: ~50% lower hernia formation rates when used at stoma creation.
Rare Abdominal Wall Hernias

While inguinal, femoral, umbilical, and ventral hernias are common, rare hernias are often misdiagnosed due to their atypical locations and presentations. Many of

these hernias are associated with high risks of strangulation or bowel obstruction, making early diagnosis and surgical intervention critical.

Types of Rare Abdominal Wall Hernias
1️- Interparietal Hernia
  • Definition: The hernia sac lies between the layers of the abdominal wall, rather than protruding outward.
  • Clinical Features:
  • Often mistaken for tumors or abscesses.
  • High risk of obstruction or strangulation.
  • Diagnosis:
  • CT scan or ultrasound shows bowel trapped within the abdominal wall layers.
  • Treatment:
  • Surgical repair as soon as diagnosed due to the risk of strangulation.
2️- Spigelian Hernia
  • Definition: A hernia through the linea semilunaris (lateral border of rectus sheath), typically above the inferior epigastric vessels.
  • Clinical Features:
  • Localized pain in the lateral abdomen, worsened by activity.
  • Difficult to detect on physical exam since it may lie under the external oblique muscle.
  • Diagnosis:
  • Ultrasound or CT scan (Valsalva maneuver may help).
  • Treatment:
  • High risk of incarceration → surgical repair recommended.
  • Mesh reinforcement (especially for defects >2-3 cm).
  • Laparoscopic approach allows for bilateral evaluation and repair.
3️- Littre Hernia
  • Definition: A hernia containing a Meckel diverticulum.
  • Common Locations:
  • Inguinal (50%)
  • Femoral (20%)
  • Umbilical (20%)
  • Clinical Features:
  • Mimics Richter’s hernia (partial bowel obstruction).
  • If inflamed → presents with pain, fever, and obstruction.
  • Treatment:
  • Hernia repair + excision of Meckel’s diverticulum.
  • Separate abdominal incision if acute diverticulitis is present.
4️- Amyand Hernia
  • Definition: An inguinal hernia containing the appendix.
  • Clinical Features:
  • Can present with or without appendicitis.
  • If appendicitis is present → resembles incarcerated inguinal hernia.
  • Treatment:
  • Appendectomy + hernia repair with native tissue (no mesh if infection is present).
  • If the appendix is normal, it can be left in place, and mesh repair is performed.
5️- Lumbar Hernia (Grynfeltt or Petit Hernia)
  • Definition: A posterior abdominal wall hernia through the lumbar region.
  • Common Locations:
  • Superior lumbar triangle (Grynfeltt’s hernia)
  • Inferior lumbar triangle (Petit’s hernia)
  • Clinical Features:
  • Flank bulge that increases with standing.
  • Dull, pulling sensation in the lower back.
  • Diagnosis:
  • CT scan to confirm hernia and differentiate from abscess, hematoma, or renal tumor.
  • Treatment:
  • Open or laparoscopic repair.
  • Mesh reinforcement is preferred for larger defects.
6️- Obturator Hernia
  • Definition: A hernia through the obturator canal, most common in elderly, thin women.
  • Clinical Features:
  • Often asymptomatic until bowel obstruction occurs.
  • Howship-Romberg sign: Pain radiating down the inner thigh (due to obturator nerve compression).
  • Diagnosis:
  • CT scan (high suspicion in elderly women with unexplained small bowel obstruction).
  • Treatment:
  • Emergency surgery required (high risk of strangulation).
  • Laparoscopic or open repair with mesh.
7️- Perineal Hernia
  • Definition: A hernia through the pelvic floor, often following pelvic surgery (e.g., abdominoperineal resection, prostatectomy).
  • Clinical Features:
  • Bulge in the perineum, often painless but can cause bowel obstruction or skin breakdown.
  • Treatment:
  • Abdominal approach for repair.
  • Mesh or muscle flaps (gracilis, rectus abdominis, gluteus) if primary repair is not feasible.
8- Sciatic Hernia
  • Definition: Herniation of abdominal contents through the greater sciatic foramen.
  • Clinical Features:
  • Pelvic pain + bowel obstruction (often diagnosed late).
  • Diagnosis:
  • CT or MRI to confirm.
  • Treatment:
  • Abdominal repair with mesh reinforcement.
9️- Traumatic Hernia
  • Definition: Herniation caused by blunt abdominal trauma, leading to fascia rupture.
  • Clinical Features:
  • Abdominal ecchymosis + bulging mass.
  • May be difficult to detect initially.
  • Diagnosis:
  • CT scan to confirm defect and rule out intra-abdominal injuries.
  • Treatment:
  • Primary repair if possible.
  • Mesh reinforcement for large defects.
  • Definitive repair is sometimes delayed until after initial recovery.
Abdominal Wall Trauma, Pain, and Tumors
Congenital Defects of the Abdominal Wall

While congenital hernias, urachal remnants, and umbilical anomalies are common, other congenital defects of the abdominal wall are rare. These are often diagnosed early in life and may require surgical intervention depending on the severity of the defect.

Traumatic Abdominal Wall Injuries
1️- Rectus Sheath Hematoma
  • Definition: A localized hematoma within the rectus abdominis muscle, often due to trauma, anticoagulation, or vascular diseases.
  • Clinical Features:
  • Severe localized abdominal pain, either sudden or progressive.
  • Tender mass in the abdominal wall, which becomes more distinct when the patient tenses the abdominal muscles (Fothergill’s sign).
  • Ecchymosis or skin discoloration may be present.
  • Diagnosis:
  • Ultrasound or CT scan to confirm hematoma and rule out intra- abdominal pathology.
  • Treatment:
  • Supportive management (pain control, rest, ice, compression).
  • Correct coagulation abnormalities (if present).
  • Rarely requires surgery → Interventional embolization if bleeding persists.
Abdominal Wall Pain Syndromes
1️- Causes of Localized Abdominal Wall Pain
  • Nerve entrapment (from nonabsorbable sutures or scars).
  • Post-surgical pain (especially in the first 6 months after surgery).
  • Herniated nerves or small occult hernias.
  • Referred pain from spinal cord injuries, diaphragm, or herpes zoster (shingles).
  • Diagnosis:
  • Pain worsens with abdominal wall contraction (distinguishes from intra-abdominal causes).
  • MRI or CT scan to rule out occult hernia or other pathology.
  • Local anesthetic nerve block can confirm nerve-related pain.
  • Treatment:
  • Nerve block with alcohol or nerve excision if severe pain persists.
  • Surgical correction of hernia (if present).
  • Pain management with NSAIDs or local anesthetics.
Abdominal Wall Tumors
1️- Benign Abdominal Wall Tumors
  • Types:
  • Lipomas (most common, soft, mobile fat tumors).
  • Hemangiomas (vascular tumors, may be bluish or pulsatile).
  • Fibromas (firm, slow-growing connective tissue tumors).
  • Desmoid tumors (fibromatoses):
    • Aggressive benign tumors from musculoaponeurotic tissue.
    • Common after pregnancy or abdominal surgery.
    • Locally invasive, but do not metastasize.
    • Surgical excision or targeted therapy for symptomatic cases.
2️- Malignant Abdominal Wall Tumors
  • Most common cause: Metastases from intra-abdominal or distant primary tumors.
  • Common primary sources:
  • Pancreatic cancer.
  • Lung cancer.
  • Intra-abdominal tumors with direct invasion.
  • Clinical Features:
  • Rapidly growing painful nodules in the abdominal wall.
  • Firm, non-mobile masses that do not transilluminate.
  • May present with systemic cancer symptoms (weight loss, fatigue, night sweats).
  • Diagnosis:
  • CT scan or MRI for detailed imaging.
  • Biopsy (core needle biopsy or excisional biopsy) for histopathology.
  • Treatment:
  • Surgical excision for resectable tumors.
  • Chemotherapy or radiation for metastatic or locally aggressive tumors.
